# Delay differential equations {#sec-delay-differential-equations}

Every population model so far in this course — the ODE of @sec-foundations,
the jump process, and the stochastic differential equation — assumes an
infectious period that is **exponentially distributed**: recovery happens at a
constant hazard $\gamma$, memoryless of how long an individual has already
been infectious. A delay differential equation (DDE) replaces that assumption
with the opposite extreme: every infectious period lasts *exactly* the same
fixed duration $\tau$. This appendix builds that model, explains the *method
of steps* used to solve it, and shows numerically how much the shape of the
infectious-period distribution — not just its mean — changes epidemic
dynamics.

## Learning goals

By the end of this unit you should be able to:

- classify a DDE model and explain how a fixed recovery delay differs from
  the memoryless recovery of @sec-foundations;
- write a DDE for SIR dynamics using a history function for states before the
  start time;
- construct a `DDEProblem` with `DelayDiffEq` and solve it with
  `MethodOfSteps`, declaring the constant lag for solver efficiency;
- explain the method of steps and why declaring lags helps the solver locate
  derivative discontinuities; and
- cross-validate a single DDE run against an equivalent two-stage
  (ODE-then-DDE) construction, and compare the result with the exponential
  recovery model.

## Model assumptions and classification

The population is the same closed, homogeneously mixing cohort used
throughout the course: $N = 1000$, $S(0) = 990$, $I(0) = 10$, $R(0) = 0$,
contact rate $c = 10$, and per-contact transmission probability $\beta =
0.05$. The only change from @eq-ch01-sir is *how long an infection lasts*:
instead of an exponential holding time with rate $\gamma$, every individual
infected at time $t^{*}$ recovers at exactly $t^{*} + \tau$, with
$\tau = 1/\gamma = 4$ chosen so the *mean* infectious period matches the rest
of the course.

| Property | Classification |
|---|---|
| Determinism | Deterministic |
| Time | Continuous |
| State | Continuous |
| Infectious period | Fixed delay $\tau$ (degenerate distribution, coefficient of variation 0) |

This is still a **deterministic, continuous-time, continuous-state,
population-level** model — the same category as @sec-foundations — but it is
no longer a Markovian ODE, because the rate of recovery at time $t$ depends on
the state *at time $t-\tau$*, not just the state at time $t$.

## Equations

Let $\lambda(t) = \beta c\, I(t)/N(t)$ be the force of infection at time $t$.
New infections at time $t$ occur at rate $\lambda(t) S(t)$; each of those
individuals recovers exactly $\tau$ time units later, so the *recovery* flow
at time $t$ equals the *infection* flow at time $t - \tau$:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\lambda(t) S(t), \qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \lambda(t) S(t) - \lambda(t-\tau) S(t-\tau), \qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}t} = \lambda(t-\tau) S(t-\tau).
$$ {#eq-a01-dde}

Because @eq-a01-dde reaches back to $t - \tau$, it needs a **history
function** $h(t)$ supplying $\bigl(S(t), I(t), R(t)\bigr)$ for all $t \le 0$,
not just a single initial vector. We assume everyone was susceptible before
the simulation starts,

$$
h(t) = (N, 0, 0), \qquad t \le 0,
$$ {#eq-a01-history}

and let the $I(0) = 10$ initial infections enter as a discontinuous jump at
$t=0$ — they are treated as having been infected at $t=0$ itself, so
@eq-a01-history correctly gives zero recoveries while $t < \tau$ (since
$t - \tau < 0$ there, and the history has no infected individuals).

**Method of steps.** A DDE with a single constant lag $\tau$ can be solved by
repeatedly treating it as an ODE: on $[0, \tau]$ the delayed term $S(t-\tau),
I(t-\tau)$ is fully determined by the *known* history $h$, so @eq-a01-dde is
an ordinary ODE there. Once that segment is solved, the dense solution on
$[0, \tau]$ becomes the exact "history" needed to solve the next segment
$[\tau, 2\tau]$, and so on. Derivative discontinuities introduced by the
history mismatch at $t=0$ propagate forward at $t = \tau, 2\tau, 3\tau,
\dots$, growing smoother at each step. Declaring the lag via `constant_lags`
tells the solver exactly where to expect these breakpoints, so it can place a
step boundary there instead of discovering the discontinuity through failed
error control.

## Julia implementation

The current `DelayDiffEq.jl` represents the delayed state through a history
function `h(p, t)` passed as the third argument of the right-hand side, and
solves the resulting `DDEProblem` with `MethodOfSteps`, which wraps any
`OrdinaryDiffEq` algorithm.

```{julia}
#| label: code-a01-setup
using DelayDiffEq
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using CairoMakie
```

```{julia}
#| label: code-a01-kernel
function sir_dde!(du, u, h, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    β, c, τ = p
    N = S + I + R
    λ = β * c * I / N                  # eq-a01-dde, current force of infection
    Sd, Id, Rd = h(p, t - τ)           # delayed state at t - τ
    Nd = Sd + Id + Rd
    λd = β * c * Id / Nd               # delayed force of infection
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - λd * Sd
    du[3] = λd * Sd
    return nothing
end

sir_history(p, t) = [1000.0, 0.0, 0.0]     # eq-a01-history: fully susceptible before t=0

u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]
γ = 0.25
p = (0.05, 10.0, 1 / γ)                    # β, c, τ = 1/γ = 4.0
tspan = (0.0, 40.0)

prob_dde = DDEProblem(sir_dde!, u0, sir_history, tspan, p; constant_lags = [p[3]])
sol_dde = solve(prob_dde, MethodOfSteps(Tsit5()); reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
round.(sol_dde.u[end]; digits = 2)
```

### An independent two-stage construction

Because there are no recoveries before $t = \tau$, the system on $[0, \tau]$
is exactly an SI ODE (no `R` flow). Solving that ODE first and using its dense
output as the history for a *second* `DDEProblem` starting at $t=\tau$ gives a
numerically independent route to the same trajectory — useful both as a
cross-check and as a template for models whose early history is not as simple
as "everybody susceptible".

```{julia}
#| label: code-a01-alt
function si_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I = u[1], u[2]
    β, c, _ = p
    λ = β * c * I / (u[1] + u[2] + u[3])
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S
    du[3] = 0.0
    return nothing
end

prob_si = ODEProblem(si_ode!, u0, (0.0, p[3]), p)
sol_si = solve(prob_si, Tsit5(); reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-10)

history_from_ode(p, t) = sol_si(t)
prob_dde2 = DDEProblem(sir_dde!, sol_si(p[3]), history_from_ode, (p[3], tspan[2]), p;
                        constant_lags = [p[3]])
sol_dde2 = solve(prob_dde2, MethodOfSteps(Tsit5()); reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
round.(sol_dde2.u[end]; digits = 2)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-a01-trajectories
#| fig-cap: "Fixed-delay DDE trajectory (solid) compared with the exponential-recovery ODE of @sec-ordinary-differential-equations (dashed infectious curve). The vertical line marks the fixed recovery delay τ. The DDE produces a taller, sharper peak because every infection lasts exactly τ time units instead of an exponentially varying time."
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    β, c, γrate = p
    N = S + I + R
    λ = β * c * I / N
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - γrate * I
    du[3] = γrate * I
    return nothing
end
sol_ode = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, (0.05, 10.0, γ)), Tsit5();
                 reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)

tt = 0.0:0.2:40.0
fig = Figure(size = (720, 440))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time", ylabel = "number",
          title = "Fixed-delay (DDE) vs exponential (ODE) recovery")
lines!(ax, tt, [sol_dde(t)[1] for t in tt]; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3, label = "S (DDE)")
lines!(ax, tt, [sol_dde(t)[2] for t in tt]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "I (DDE)")
lines!(ax, tt, [sol_dde(t)[3] for t in tt]; color = :seagreen, linewidth = 3, label = "R (DDE)")
lines!(ax, tt, [sol_ode(t)[2] for t in tt]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2,
       linestyle = :dash, label = "I (ODE)")
vlines!(ax, [p[3]]; color = :black, linestyle = :dot, label = "τ")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

## Validation

**Cross-check.** The single-history and two-stage constructions must agree
everywhere, since they solve the same mathematical problem two different
ways:

```{julia}
#| label: code-a01-check-crosscheck
grid = 0.0:0.5:40.0
diffs = [maximum(abs.(sol_dde(t) .- (t < p[3] ? sol_si(t) : sol_dde2(t)))) for t in grid]
maximum(diffs) < 1e-4
```

**Conservation and non-negativity.** The population total must stay at $N$
and every compartment must remain nonnegative:

```{julia}
#| label: code-a01-check-conservation
ts_dense = 0.0:0.1:40.0
states = [sol_dde(t) for t in ts_dense]
conserved = all(u -> isapprox(sum(u), 1000.0; atol = 1e-6), states)
nonnegative = all(u -> all(>=(-1e-8), u), states)
(conserved, nonnegative)
```

**Structural comparison.** Both models share the same mean infectious period
$1/\gamma = \tau = 4$, yet the fixed delay produces a substantially higher
infectious peak than the exponential-recovery ODE:

```{julia}
#| label: code-a01-check-peak
peak_dde = maximum(sol_dde[2, :])
peak_ode = maximum(sol_ode[2, :])
(round(peak_dde; digits = 1), round(peak_ode; digits = 1), peak_dde > peak_ode)
```

All three checks return `true`: the two DDE constructions agree to solver
tolerance, the trajectory conserves $N$ and stays nonnegative, and the fixed
delay yields the higher, sharper peak predicted by epidemic theory.

## Interpretation and limitations

The gap between the two peaks in the validation section is not a numerical
artifact — it reflects a real, well-known sensitivity of epidemic dynamics to
the *shape*, not just the mean, of the infectious-period distribution. A fixed
delay has zero variance (coefficient of variation 0): nobody recovers early,
so the initial cohort keeps transmitting at full strength throughout $[0,
\tau)$ before disappearing all at once. Exponential recovery has the same
mean but a coefficient of variation of 1, so many individuals recover quickly
and temper the early growth. Real infectious periods usually sit between
these two extremes; the model-composition appendix's Erlang (linear chain)
construction is one common way to interpolate between them within ordinary
differential equations, avoiding the delay machinery altogether for that
class of distributions.

Numerically, `MethodOfSteps` is only as efficient as the lag information you
give it: omitting `constant_lags` still produces a correct answer for a
constant delay, but the adaptive step-size controller must rediscover the
breakpoints at $\tau, 2\tau, \dots$ by trial and error, which is slower and can
be less accurate near those points. The history discontinuity at $t=0$ is a
genuine limitation of the "instant seeding" convention used here: it assumes
all initial infections happened simultaneously, which is convenient but not
realistic; the two-stage construction above shows how to relax that
assumption by supplying a more detailed history function. Finally, this
remains a population-level, deterministic model: it has no demographic
noise, so the SDDE built on it in the next appendix is needed whenever
finite-population fluctuations matter.

For the full API, see the
[DelayDiffEq.jl documentation](https://docs.sciml.ai/DelayDiffEq/stable/) and
the
[SciML DDE problem reference](https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/types/dde_types/).
For the classical role of infectious-period distributions in epidemic
dynamics see @andersonmay1991.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#a01-ex1}

Solve the DDE model for $\tau \in \{2, 4, 8\}$ (holding $\beta$, $c$, and $N$
fixed) and record the peak infectious count and the time at which it occurs
for each. Compare with the peak of the exponential-recovery ODE at the
matching mean infectious period $1/\gamma = \tau$. Describe how the size and
timing of the gap between the two models changes as $\tau$ grows.

### Exercise 2 {#a01-ex2}

The single-history construction in this appendix seeds all $I(0)=10$ initial
infections as happening exactly at $t=0$. Repeat the two-stage construction
(presolve, then continue as a DDE) for $I(0) = 1$ initial infection instead of
10, and confirm that the resulting trajectory still conserves the population
and stays nonnegative. Then add a `ContinuousCallback` that would clamp $I$ to
zero if it ever went negative, run the model, and report whether the callback
ever fires. Explain why it should not, in contrast to the stochastic delay
model of the next appendix.
